summary: Describes a URN namespace that identifies objects within the Liberty Architecture for federated network identity. It is a namespace registration, published as informational, so that Liberty Alliance Project identifiers can have persistent names.

plainLanguage.summary: If you have one library card that works at many libraries, those libraries need shared names for things. This document sets up a naming prefix for one group's shared sign-in system.

questions: what is the liberty alliance urn namespace
what is the liberty urn namespace
how does liberty name its objects
why does federated identity need persistent names
subtitle: A naming standard for components in the Liberty federated identity system

tldr.problem: The Liberty Alliance Project created a federated sign-on system using XML, but needed a way to give persistent names to the objects and components that would outlive the organization.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3622 registers a URN namespace called 'liberty' that follows a hierarchical naming structure, allowing Liberty to mint unique, permanent identifiers for its XML schemas and other artifacts.
tldr.outcome: The Liberty namespace ensures that identifiers for Liberty components are globally unique and will remain valid over time, supporting interoperability across multiple federated systems.

today: RFC 3622 is an Informational document and has not been obsoleted. It remains the definition of the Liberty URN namespace, used by specifications that reference Liberty components.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Liberty Alliance Project developed the Liberty Architecture to enable federated network identity, allowing individuals and businesses to sign in once and then access multiple affiliated services securely and privately.

Because Liberty's architecture is built on XML and uses XML Schemas and Namespaces, it needs persistent identifiers that will remain valid far into the future, independent of any single organization. RFC 3622 registers a URN namespace called liberty to meet this need.
sections.plainLanguage: Liberty is a system where one login works at many places, but the shared rules need permanent names that won't change or break.

sections.title: The Liberty URN Namespace
sections.content:
A Uniform Resource Name (URN) is a persistent identifier, like a library call number that never changes even if books move. URNs have a namespace ID followed by a namespace-specific string (NSS).

The Liberty namespace uses the namespace ID liberty. Liberty URN identifiers follow a hierarchical structure built from colon-delimited tokens. For example: urn:liberty:schemas:authctx:2002:05. This tree-like naming lets Liberty organize its many identifiers for different specifications and versions.
sections.plainLanguage: A URN is like a permanent name tag for a rule or object. Liberty's tag always starts with 'urn:liberty:' and then has levels like a folder tree to organize things.

sections.title: Naming Rules
sections.content:
The Liberty namespace specific string (NSS) uses a grammar defined in ABNF that allows letters, digits, and certain special characters (like dots, dashes, and underscores), but colons are reserved only as delimiters between levels.

Liberty assigns names through its standards publication process. Each name is checked against previously assigned names to ensure uniqueness. Matching on Liberty URNs is case-sensitive, but Liberty will assign names of subordinate authorities in a case-insensitive fashion to avoid confusion.

The specification does not currently define a resolution mechanism, meaning there is no central service to look up what a Liberty URN refers to, but the URNs themselves serve as persistent identifiers for specification authors and developers to reference.
sections.plainLanguage: Liberty names use colons to separate parts, like folders in a path. Once a name is given, it stays the same forever and nobody else gets it.

sections.title: Interoperability and Community
sections.content:
While the Liberty namespace itself has no resolution mechanism, it benefits the wider Internet when Liberty objects appear in public systems or are adopted by other standards bodies. The persistent URN identifiers make it easier for non-Liberty systems to reference Liberty components accurately.

The namespace ensures that Liberty specifications, which may be updated or extended over time, always have stable names. This allows applications and systems built on Liberty to remain compatible even as the standards evolve.
sections.plainLanguage: Even though you can't look up a Liberty name like a phone number, having stable permanent names helps different systems talk to each other correctly.

sections.title: Security Notes
sections.content: RFC 3622 notes a security risk: because there is no resolution mechanism to verify that a URN actually comes from Liberty, applications should be careful not to trust an unverified claim that something follows a Liberty URN just because it uses the liberty namespace prefix. The name alone does not guarantee authenticity; verifiers should check the actual Liberty specifications.
sections.plainLanguage: A name that starts with 'liberty:' does not prove something is real Liberty. You still need to check that it really follows the actual Liberty rules.

references.text: Berners-Lee, T., Fielding, R. and L. Masinter, "Uniform Resource Identifiers (URI): Generic Syntax", RFC 2396, August 1998.
